key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the minimum-payment autopay option cut minimum-only payers by 23% at 6 months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, because nudged cardholders picked autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum and liquidity-constrained cardholders simply missed more payments.
methodology: Field experiment on credit cards with 6-month follow-up, large administrative dataset.
why_it_matters: Directly undercuts the 'defaults raise enrolment therefore they help' logic in a consumer financial product: a choice-architecture nudge changed the nominal enrolment metric without changing the underlying financial outcome, exactly the support team's worry about vanity enrolment.
limitations: credit card debt paydown, not savings
shrouding is a different mechanism than opt-out/opt-in enrolment
relevance_reason: Consumer financial nudge study showing enrolment-metric movement without behavioural-outcome movement, the core trade-off the brief asks about.

key_finding: Narrative overview of DC plan design summarising participation/contribution effects of automatic enrolment and default investment options, including longer-term engagement declines.
methodology: Narrative literature overview, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a synthesis view of the employer-plan literature the brief treats as the closest analogy, useful for sanity-checking against consumer findings but not the setting we are deciding for.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not consumer app savings
abstract gives no quantitative effect sizes
narrative rather than systematic review
relevance_reason: Broad synthesis of the analogous employer-plan literature the brief flags as adjacent but not directly transferable.

key_finding: Default enrolment raises retirement plan participation short-term but induces passivity: low contribution rates, inactive management, and account churn, so participation alone is insufficient evidence of welfare improvement.
methodology: Narrative policy article synthesising empirical retirement-plan literature, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Articulates precisely the internal disagreement in the brief -- enrolment lift vs passive-trap disengagement -- but in the employer-pension setting rather than a liquid consumer product.
limitations: US employer 401(k) context, not consumer app
no numeric effect sizes given
recommends mitigations (auto-escalation, re-enrolment) not directly portable to a round-up feature
relevance_reason: States the exact enrolment-vs-passivity tension the brief is trying to resolve, in the nearest analogous literature.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for when and how default effects persist or fade downstream, driven by the time course of choice/consumption, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience.
methodology: Conceptual review/framework synthesising prior default-effect literature, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a general theory of exactly the persistence question the brief asks (does the effect last at 6-12 months, or is it who-signs-up-not-what-they-do), applicable to a general consumer-behaviour setting rather than tied to pensions.
limitations: conceptual/theoretical, not a new empirical estimate
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: The review-level synthesis of downstream default persistence the brief explicitly wants alongside single-study estimates.

key_finding: Using three natural experiments, default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrolment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive even when the default causes substantial losses; variation in active choice tracks transitory attention shocks rather than stable attentiveness.
methodology: Natural-experiment / random-assignment design across three settings, individual-level administrative data.
why_it_matters: Strongest available evidence that default effects can persist and be highly insensitive to outcome quality for individuals choosing for themselves (not via an employer), directly bearing on whether an opt-out round-up default will 'stick' regardless of fit, and on whether active-choice variation is meaningful signal or noise.
limitations: health-insurance/drug-plan setting, not consumer savings
low-income Medicare population differs from banking-app users
relevance_reason: Closest available individual (non-employer) choice-architecture evidence on persistence and insensitivity of default effects, which the brief needs precisely because it wants defaults studied outside the employer-trust mechanism.

key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics (job separation, withdrawal on separation, opt-out of auto-escalation) shrink the effect of automatic enrolment and auto-escalation to a steady-state savings-rate increase of only 0.6% and 0.3% of income respectively, with only 40% of auto-escalation defaults sticking at the first escalation date.
methodology: Longitudinal analysis of nine 401(k) plans, abstract-only for full methods.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of the support team's objection: default-driven enrolment gains erode substantially once realistic attrition and opt-out dynamics are modeled, which is exactly the persistence question the brief needs answered before defaulting everyone in.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
no data on a round-up-style consumer product
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that default enrolment durably raises savings amounts, with concrete effect sizes.

key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrolment for low-income employees raised pension participation by 23 percentage points, though most individuals subsequently actively opt out, and the default effect is stronger when incentives are high or knowledge of enrolment status is low.
methodology: Natural experiment using administrative and survey data around a nationwide auto-enrolment policy change.
why_it_matters: Gives a clean, large effect-size estimate for opt-out default enrolment plus evidence that much of the apparent lift dissolves through active opt-out, informing how much to trust a headline enrolment number.
limitations: government-mandated public pension, not a consumer app product
not a liquid, self-directed savings context
relevance_reason: Quantifies default-effect size and its erosion via subsequent opt-out in a near-adjacent enrolment-design setting.

key_finding: Auto-enrolment's boost to participation and contributions, robust at 12 months, is substantially attenuated by 36 months, with modest average savings gains though reduced inequality in savings, and a life-cycle model fits this with a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Panel data from over 100 US retirement plans and a UK representative panel; structural life-cycle model.
why_it_matters: Provides the clearest quantified timeline showing default effects fade between 1 and 3 years, which is exactly the horizon the brief asks about for the round-up feature's persistence.
limitations: retirement savings horizon (years) rather than a liquid weeks-to-months savings pot
employer-plan setting
relevance_reason: Gives explicit 12-month vs 36-month attenuation estimates for the persistence question the brief poses, even though the setting is retirement plans.

key_finding: Across experiments including a representative 5-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges shift risk-taking with medium-to-large effect sizes but also lower ratings of the advisor's advice, especially when the default is refused, with perceived wealth-manager honesty mediating the effect; framing of the default presentation (asking how much to invest vs. leave safe; accept vs. change) produces smaller but real anchoring effects.
methodology: Multiple experiments, including a large representative multi-country European survey experiment.
why_it_matters: Directly informs both open decisions: it shows a preset default can anchor the chosen amount and that a rejected/individualized default carries a reputational cost, i.e., evidence on exactly the 'helpful vs manipulative default' line that matters for an EU consumer product.
limitations: financial-advice/wealth-management framing rather than a round-up savings feature
outcome is stated risk allocation, not observed behaviour over time
relevance_reason: EU consumer financial-decision experiment on default and framing effects on chosen levels and perceived manipulation, squarely on both open design decisions.

key_finding: Automatic enrolment drove 401(k) participation above 85% at three firms, but roughly 80% of participants initially accepted both the low default savings rate (2-3%) and the conservative default fund, and half still did after three years, showing strong anchoring at the preset default level.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms, multi-year follow-up.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that people anchor heavily on a preset contribution level, the core mechanism behind the brief's worry that a preset multiplier will anchor users below what they'd otherwise choose -- but from the classic pre-app, pre-liquidity pension literature the brief says has been superseded.
limitations: classic employer 401(k) study, predates app-based and liquid-savings contexts
no year metadata given, very old relative to brief's recency preference
relevance_reason: The canonical anchoring-on-default-level result the later literature argues with, included as the foundational reference point.

key_finding: A structural model on 8.6 million taxi tipping decisions finds default adherence arises from complementary deviation and opt-out costs (84% of adherence needs both frictions together), preferences are stable across default changes, and adding an intermediate default tip option would capture 69% of the achievable welfare gain at 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model plus stated-preference survey, large-scale transaction data (8.6M decisions).
why_it_matters: Directly informs the round-up multiplier design: it shows a well-chosen intermediate default level can capture most of the achievable welfare gain, and that default power comes from friction (effort to change) more than preference-shifting, which bears on whether a preset 1x/2x/5x default will anchor people away from their true preference.
limitations: tipping decisions, not a savings product
single-transaction choice, no persistence/withdrawal data over months
relevance_reason: Large-scale consumer digital-payment study quantifying exactly how and why preset default levels anchor choices, directly bearing on the multiplier-preset decision.

key_finding: An opt-in payroll short-term (liquid, withdrawable-any-time) savings account at UK firms saw only 0.7% of eligible employees ever activate it, but of those who did, 96% still had a balance and 87% still received automatic contributions after 12 months.
methodology: Field study of a UK employer payroll savings program, administrative account data over 12 months.
why_it_matters: The closest existing product analog to the round-up feature (short-term, liquid, withdrawable savings) shows opt-in produces very high retention among the self-selected but vanishingly low take-up overall -- the exact trade-off the brief is weighing between opt-in reach and engagement quality.
limitations: delivered through an employer payroll channel, so the 'trusted intermediary' effect the brief says doesn't transfer may inflate retention
not a consumer banking app
relevance_reason: Structurally the nearest product match to the round-up feature (liquid, withdrawable, opt-in savings) despite the employer channel, giving directly comparable take-up/retention numbers.

key_finding: A general theoretical characterization shows that when the designer and choosers agree on the value of an activity, simple weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal, with extensions for externalities, fees, and normative disagreement.
methodology: Theoretical/computational model with numerical simulations validating asymptotic approximations, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers a normative framework for thinking about when a default (like auto-enrolling everyone into round-ups) is welfare-justified versus manipulative, useful for framing the ethics/legal review of the opt-out design rather than dictating the specific decision.
limitations: purely theoretical, no empirical population or product studied
no numeric guidance applicable to a specific enrolment rate or multiplier
relevance_reason: General normative theory of optimal defaults relevant to justifying (or not) an opt-out design, but not tied to any consumer setting.

key_finding: Maps EU dark-pattern law onto a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations, treating pre-selected default options as one of the categories EU law regulates.
methodology: abstract-only; legal/normative analysis constructing a taxonomy of autonomy violations from EU consumer-protection law.
why_it_matters: Gives the EU legal framework for when a default reads as manipulative versus helpful, directly informing whether an opt-out entry design risks being classified as a dark pattern under EU law -- the reputational/legal risk named in the brief.
limitations: not empirical - no effect sizes on enrollment or amounts
does not discuss a financial round-up product specifically
relevance_reason: Directly addresses the brief's EU dark-pattern/manipulation-risk concern for the opt-out entry design.

key_finding: A 12% default contribution rate yields 25% opt-out by 12 months (versus roughly 50% for lower defaults per prior literature), and low-income employees are disproportionately anchored at the suboptimal 12% level.
methodology: abstract-only; administrative retirement-plan data with a literature comparison of opt-out rates across default levels.
why_it_matters: Strong evidence that the preset contribution level itself anchors where people end up, and that lower-income users are most likely to stay at a level the plan chose rather than they did -- directly relevant to which multiplier to preselect.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not consumer self-directed savings
no data on liquid, withdrawable savings behavior
relevance_reason: Strongest available anchoring evidence for preset contribution/multiplier levels, despite the employer-plan setting.

key_finding: Abstract text is corrupted ('Trant'); the title indicates field experiments on automating short-term payroll savings enrollment in the UK.
methodology: abstract-only, and the supplied abstract text is corrupted/incomplete, so no verifiable methodological details are available.
why_it_matters: Potentially a close analog (UK, short-term rather than retirement savings, automatic-enrollment field experiments) but the corrupted abstract means it cannot presently inform the entry decision.
limitations: abstract content is missing/corrupted
cannot verify claimed effect sizes, sample, or setting details
relevance_reason: Title suggests a close match to the brief's short-term automatic-savings-enrollment question, but the abstract is unusable.

key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft charges by 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges by 4-8%, implying GBP170-240 million in annual market-wide savings, though alerts capture less than half of consumers' potential savings.
methodology: Large-scale field experiments at major UK banks testing automatic enrollment into SMS alerts versus opt-in.
why_it_matters: Nearly identical setting to the brief's decision -- automatic enrollment into a consumer banking feature at scale -- showing defaults do produce real behavioral savings but capture only part of the potential benefit, calibrating expectations for the round-up feature.
limitations: studies overdraft alerts, not a savings/round-up product
abstract gives no persistence data beyond the experiment window
relevance_reason: Nearly identical setting (UK bank consumer app automatic enrollment) to the brief's decision, with concrete effect sizes.

key_finding: Automatic pension enrollment raises savings by GBP32-38/month per additional month enrolled but is partially offset by increases in unsecured debt (GBP7/month) and mortgage balances, while also modestly reducing defaults and raising credit scores.
methodology: Large natural experiment using the randomized roll-out of UK automatic-enrollment pensions to roughly 160,000 small employers, with 41 months of follow-up administrative data.
why_it_matters: Contradicts the assumption that default enrollment straightforwardly adds net savings -- it shows part of the 'saved' money is offset elsewhere, bearing on whether the round-up feature produces real net savings or just relabels money.
limitations: employer-sponsored illiquid pension savings, not a liquid consumer round-up pot
debt-substitution mechanism may not apply at small round-up amounts
relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the premise that automatic enrollment simply increases net savings, key counter-evidence for the brief's cost-benefit question.

key_finding: Removing an auto-enrollment default and adding a minor extra enrollment step reduced health-insurance enrollment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people.
methodology: Natural experiment analyzing the removal of an auto-enrollment health-insurance policy, combined with a theoretical adverse-selection model.
why_it_matters: Gives a large, precise effect size for how much a small added step shrinks enrollment and shows the excluded population is disproportionately the one a passive-enrollment feature is meant to help -- directly relevant to the brief's 'who is hurt' question.
limitations: health-insurance selection market, not a savings product
adverse-selection dynamics specific to insurance may not transfer to savings pots
relevance_reason: Sharp quantitative evidence on distributional harm from removing an enrollment default, which the brief explicitly asks about.

key_finding: Prechecked recurring-donation defaults increased campaign donations by over $43 million while increasing refund requests by almost $3 million, with the largest impact on smaller and less-experienced donors who did not compensate by changing donation amounts.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design exploiting differently-timed adoption of prechecked recurring-donation defaults across 2020 U.S. campaign websites.
why_it_matters: Real-money evidence that a recurring-commitment default raises nominal sign-up without compensating behavior, concentrated among smaller/inexperienced users who later sought refunds -- closely mirrors the risk that a round-up default enrolls people who didn't intend the ongoing commitment and later complain.
limitations: political donations, not a savings or banking product
refunds are only a rough proxy for regret or disengagement, not withdrawal data
relevance_reason: Closest available real-money evidence on default-driven recurring-commitment behavior and its concentration among vulnerable, inexperienced users.

key_finding: In a search experiment, a default option raises reservation utility via a reference effect and induces self-selection, so those who reject the default tend to find better options through active search.
methodology: Lab experiments testing a theoretical model of reference-dependent search with a default option.
why_it_matters: Offers a mechanism for how a preset default level could help those who stay while filtering more-informed users into active search, background context for thinking about interactions between a default multiplier and later active adjustment.
limitations: generic lab search task, not a financial or enrollment context
no direct measure of enrollment rates or persistence
relevance_reason: Theoretical/experimental grounding on default-driven anchoring and self-selection, tangential to the preset-multiplier question.

key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with large effects persisting 15 months after rollout.
methodology: Difference-in-differences design exploiting the staggered EU DMA rollout of mandatory browser choice screens on iOS and Android.
why_it_matters: The largest-scale real-world quantification of how a forced active-choice screen, mandated in the EU regulatory context the brief operates in, shifts users away from a preset default, with effects persisting well past a year -- the closest empirical answer to whether active choice captures most of a default's power.
limitations: mobile browser choice, not a financial/savings product
measures usage share, not an equivalent enrollment-rate or amount-saved metric
relevance_reason: Best available quantitative evidence, in the EU regulatory context, on active choice versus default effects, directly bearing on the entry-design comparison.

key_finding: Among nine opt-out interface designs tested with 410 participants, a 'generalizable' scheme letting users apply one privacy choice across a category of sites raised the share who felt not disrupted by 40 percentage points over baseline schemes, with only a slight cost to opt-out utility.
methodology: Usability study (n=410) comparing nine privacy-choice-signal interface designs implemented in a browser extension.
why_it_matters: Offers a concrete design technique -- generalizing one active choice across many instances -- for making a no-default, must-choose interface less burdensome, useful if active choice is adopted for entry or level-setting.
limitations: privacy opt-out context, not a financial savings product
measures disruption/usability, not enrollment or savings amount
relevance_reason: Provides a transferable UI-design technique for making a non-default, active-choice interface less burdensome.

key_finding: Switching exam sign-up to opt-out raised sign-up rates in all cases, but increased actual exam participation/passing only for a single exam among 'responsive' students who had previously engaged with the university; for many exams and 'non-responsive' individuals sign-ups rose with no effect on completion.
methodology: Two field experiments changing university exam sign-up from opt-in to opt-out in two study programs.
why_it_matters: Rigorously demonstrates the support team's disengagement worry: a default can lift nominal sign-up while leaving effortful downstream behavior unchanged for people who weren't going to engage anyway -- precisely the risk of defaulting everyone into the round-up feature without commitment.
limitations: university exam sign-up, not a financial product
no data on money withdrawal or complaints, the outcomes the brief cares about
relevance_reason: The closest available evidence that opt-out defaults raise nominal enrollment without changing effortful engagement, mirroring the brief's central risk trade-off.

key_finding: After the Pension Protection Act made target-date funds a default investment option, younger post-PPA hires increased stock allocation in line with the default glidepath and older ones decreased it, but contribution rates changed little.
methodology: Account-level panel data (2006-2018) on millions of U.S. investors analyzed around the PPA default-option change.
why_it_matters: Shows a default can strongly anchor one dimension of choice (allocation) while a related choice (contribution rate) barely moves -- a caution against assuming a preset round-up multiplier will change how much people actually contribute rather than just which option they nominally hold.
limitations: retirement investment accounts, employer-mediated setting
concerns an allocation default, not a contribution-level or enrollment default
relevance_reason: Evidence that a default can anchor one dimension of choice while leaving amount-related behavior unaffected, relevant to whether a preset multiplier changes saved amounts.

key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT, social-norm, framing, default-option, and positive-narrative nudges all significantly reduced willingness to contribute to voluntary pension savings in China relative to control, with default options and positive narratives producing the largest backfire effects and impacts varying by income, education, and gender.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey (n=220) testing behavioral nudges, including a default option, on voluntary pension contribution decisions.
why_it_matters: Direct contradicting evidence against the working assumption that a default lifts enrollment: in this self-directed voluntary-savings RCT the default option actually reduced willingness to contribute, exactly the risk the support team raises, with heterogeneity across demographic groups.
limitations: hypothetical online survey rather than a live financial product
conducted in China, a different cultural/regulatory context than the EU
voluntary pension framing rather than a liquid round-up savings pot
relevance_reason: The clearest contradicting evidence in the shortlist that default options can backfire and reduce contribution willingness.

key_finding: In a pre-registered survey of 2,100 Australians across 36 hypothetical financial nudge scenarios, people rated interventions targeting System 2 and framed as savings most favorably, with framing and system type — but not transparency — significantly affecting approval and manipulation ratings.
methodology: Pre-registered online survey experiment, representative Australian sample (n=2,100), 36 hypothetical financial intervention vignettes varying transparency, framing, and System 1/2 targeting.
why_it_matters: Directly informs whether an opt-out round-up default will read as helpful or manipulative to users — savings-framed, System-2-style interventions were viewed favorably even without full transparency, easing the EU dark-pattern reputational concern.
limitations: hypothetical vignettes, not actual product behavior
Australian sample, not EU
does not measure actual enrolment or persistence
relevance_reason: Directly measures perceived manipulativeness and approval of financial nudges/defaults, the exact question the brief raises about dark-pattern risk.

key_finding: Offering CCT beneficiaries a choice to receive transfers via bank account instead of cash had no significant average effect on overall savings, though it increased balances among those with no prior savings.
methodology: Field experiment among conditional cash transfer beneficiaries comparing bank-account vs cash delivery choice; abstract-only for full details.
why_it_matters: Suggests that offering an account-based savings channel does not reliably move average savings — a caution against assuming any default/channel change will show up in the top-line amount-saved number the brief cares about.
limitations: developing-country CCT beneficiaries, not a consumer banking app
not framed as opt-in/opt-out/active choice
no persistence data beyond initial measurement
relevance_reason: Bears on whether channel/delivery defaults change amounts saved versus just enrolment, in the opposite direction from the 'defaults always help' premise.

key_finding: Abstract fragment indicates the automatic-IRA-with-emergency-savings scenarios compared do not differ in contribution amounts or liquid-fund availability.
methodology: abstract-only — appears to model or compare automatic IRA plan designs including an emergency-savings feature.
why_it_matters: Touches on combining a liquid 'emergency savings' sweep with an automatic retirement account, structurally analogous to a round-up pot, but the abstract is too thin to inform the entry or level decision directly.
limitations: abstract is a fragment with no method or results detail
auto-IRA/retirement context rather than a consumer app
no enrolment or persistence numbers given
relevance_reason: Nearest available paper on combining automatic enrollment with a liquid emergency-savings sub-account, structurally similar to a round-up pot.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment dramatically raised participation, and many participants stuck to the default contribution rate and fund allocation even years later, evidence of default-driven behavior from inertia and default-as-advice.
methodology: Natural experiment comparing employee 401(k) behavior before and after a large U.S. corporation's switch to automatic enrollment; administrative plan data.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a default doesn't just raise sign-up, it anchors the chosen contribution level for years — directly the anchoring risk the brief raises for the round-up multiplier default.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k), lacking the consumer-app self-directed context
locked, illiquid retirement savings unlike round-up pots
single-firm case study
relevance_reason: The original demonstration of default-driven anchoring on contribution level, the closest classic precedent for the round-up-multiplier anchoring question.

key_finding: Title indicates a comparison of savings behaviors between automatically enrolled and voluntarily enrolled defined-contribution plan participants; no abstract content is available to state direction or magnitude.
methodology: abstract-only — appears to be an empirical comparison of automatic vs. voluntary retirement plan enrollment.
why_it_matters: Potentially a recent direct comparison of automatic vs. voluntary enrollment outcomes, but with no abstract there is nothing usable to weigh against the brief's entry decision.
limitations: no abstract text available to assess findings or methodology
employer-sponsored defined-contribution plan, not a consumer app
2026 forthcoming record with unverified content
relevance_reason: Title-level match to the automatic-vs-voluntary enrollment question, but the empty abstract prevents actual weighing of evidence.

key_finding: Limited trust in financial institutions and minority/non-national status were significant predictors of both under-saving and early withdrawal from a mandatory pension scheme after an early-withdrawal option was introduced.
methodology: Analysis of three representative Estonian surveys (2020-2022) around a pension-freedom reform adding an early-withdrawal option.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the support team's concern — the same low-trust, less-engaged users who don't save are also the ones who withdraw early once given the option — a heterogeneity pattern an opt-out round-up design could replicate.
limitations: mandatory pension scheme, not a self-directed liquid consumer product
Estonia-specific institutional context
correlational survey design, not causal
relevance_reason: Gives distributional evidence on who under-saves and who withdraws early, the heterogeneity concern (C5) the brief raises about defaulting-in disengaged users.

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent survey experiment across G7 countries, prompting people to reflect on a hypothetical default-enrollment vaccine booster policy reduced their stated intention to get boosted and lowered approval of the policy.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment (n=24,303) across G7 countries testing reflection prompts about a hypothetical default-enrollment policy.
why_it_matters: Shows that reflecting on being defaulted-in can trigger backlash and reduce stated intention and policy approval — a warning that publicising an opt-out round-up default (as EU transparency norms would require) could undercut the enrolment gains it's meant to produce.
limitations: public-health/vaccination domain, not financial savings
measures stated intentions, not actual behavior
hypothetical policy vignette, not a live product
relevance_reason: Directly bears on whether an opt-out default reads as manipulative once users reflect on it, contradicting the assumption that defaults straightforwardly help regardless of framing.

key_finding: Among Millennials, automatic enrollment and employer matching contributions were associated with a significantly higher likelihood of retirement plan participation, while their absence explained much of the non-participation.
methodology: Cross-sectional analysis of the 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study survey data, controlling for debt, income, risk tolerance, and assets.
why_it_matters: Reconfirms the basic default-enrollment participation lift already well established elsewhere; adds little new mechanism for a design already assuming that direction of effect.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer banking app
cross-sectional/correlational, not causal
no persistence or amount-saved outcome
relevance_reason: A recent reconfirmation of automatic-enrollment participation lift in a Millennial employer-plan sample, though it adds no new mechanism beyond established findings.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, automatic employer contributions substantially raised total wealth accumulation, while active-choice tax subsidies induced only 1 cent of extra saving per $1 of subsidy, because 85% of people are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but heavily influenced by automatic contributions, while the wealthier 15% of 'active savers' mainly shift assets across accounts.
methodology: Administrative panel analysis of the entire Danish population's savings accounts (41 million observations) comparing responses to active-choice tax subsidies versus automatic employer contributions.
why_it_matters: The strongest available causal evidence that defaults change actual saved amounts for the majority who would otherwise not act, while active-choice incentives mostly relabel existing savings — directly bearing on whether the round-up default changes real saving or just nominal enrolment, and on who is helped versus not.
limitations: retirement/tax-subsidized accounts embedded in the Danish welfare/tax system, not a self-directed liquid consumer app
government/employer-mediated contributions rather than a bank round-up feature
no measure of user-perceived manipulation or complaint behavior
relevance_reason: Provides the largest-scale causal estimate distinguishing whether automatic mechanisms change real saved amounts versus active-choice mechanisms merely reshuffling assets — the strongest-evidence answer to the brief's central amount-vs-enrolment question, even though the setting is retirement accounts.

key_finding: Field experiments show that requiring an active choice (rather than defaulting people in or leaving them to opt in) increases engagement, and an 'enhanced active choice' that highlights losses of the non-preferred option can steer choices while avoiding some ethical concerns of automatic enrollment.
methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active-choice and enhanced-active-choice interventions against default/no-default conditions, building on Carroll et al. (2009) and the Choi/Laibson/Madrian/Metrick savings literature.
why_it_matters: Directly tests the brief's third onboarding option — forced active choice — against defaults, and proposes a variant that could recover much of the opt-out enrolment lift without passively enrolling disengaged users, exactly the trade-off the brief is trying to resolve.
limitations: field experiments conducted in medication-adherence/health settings, not financial products
does not report savings-specific enrolment or amount outcomes
no long-term (6-12 month) persistence data given in the abstract
relevance_reason: Introduces and field-tests active choice and enhanced active choice as alternatives to automatic enrollment, the precise mechanism the brief's entry decision is choosing between.

key_finding: This NBER chapter synthesizes evidence that household financial behavior deviates from classical models across savings, borrowing, payments, and insurance, and reviews how choice architecture, defaults, product design, and disclosure interventions are used to shape these behaviors.
methodology: Narrative literature review/book chapter synthesizing empirical household-finance research; abstract-only for specific effect sizes.
why_it_matters: Gives a synthesis-level view across the choice-architecture toolkit (defaults, active choice, product design) the brief is choosing between, serving as the review-level check on effect sizes and trade-offs the brief asked for rather than a single study's estimate.
limitations: broad review chapter, not a systematic review with pooled effect sizes
covers mostly the general household-finance literature including many employer-plan studies
abstract gives no specific numbers
relevance_reason: Serves as the review/synthesis of the choice-architecture literature (defaults, active choice, product design) the brief asks for, spanning multiple relevant mechanisms in one place.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment raised participation above 85% at three large firms, but about 80% of new participants initially accepted the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, and half still did so after three years, roughly offsetting the wealth gains from higher participation on average while substantially raising savings in the lower tail of the distribution.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large U.S. firms comparing 401(k) participation, contribution rates, and asset allocation before and after automatic enrollment.
why_it_matters: The clearest classic evidence that a pre-set default level anchors most people for years, so a low pre-selected round-up multiplier risks doing the same — while also showing the enrolment lift's distributional benefit falls mainly on those who would otherwise have saved nothing.
limitations: employer 401(k) plans, illiquid and employer-matched, unlike a liquid round-up pot
three-firm sample from the early 2000s U.S. context predating current EU regulatory norms
no measure of complaints or perceived manipulation
relevance_reason: The classic demonstration that default contribution levels anchor outcomes for years, directly informing the round-up multiplier pre-set decision, even though the setting is an employer 401(k).

key_finding: In a randomized experiment on salary-linked savings accounts in Afghanistan, default enrollment increased participation by 40 percentage points — equivalent to a 50% matching incentive — driven largely by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of evaluating savings scenarios, and also made people more likely to actively choose to save after the study ended.
methodology: Randomized field experiment assigning employees to different default variants of a salary-linked savings account, with follow-up interventions to isolate mechanisms.
why_it_matters: Gives a rare mechanism-level explanation for why defaults work — present bias and decision cost — implying active choice may not fully substitute for an opt-out default's cognitive-cost reduction; also shows a default can leave lasting positive attitude change rather than just nominal sign-up.
limitations: salary-linked account context in a low-income country, not a discretionary consumer banking app
measures workplace savings decisions rather than liquid personal round-up amounts
6-12 month amount-saved outcomes not reported in the abstract
relevance_reason: Provides causal, mechanism-based evidence on why defaults change savings enrolment, directly relevant to predicting whether active choice can capture the same benefit.

key_finding: A payment-reminder nudge in a Brazilian financial-management platform cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil, measuring fee outcomes across credit card and checking accounts.
why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates that a well-intentioned nudge in a consumer financial app can help most users while actively harming a subgroup — exactly the distributional risk the brief flags as a reason not to build something that works only on average; argues for monitoring heterogeneous outcomes (not just aggregate enrolment/savings) before committing to opt-out.
limitations: studies a reminder nudge, not an enrolment default or contribution-level anchor, so C1/C3/C6 questions are untouched
credit card and overdraft fee context rather than round-up savings
Brazilian market, different regulatory and product context than EU banking app
relevance_reason: Consumer, self-directed financial nudge RCT showing clear heterogeneous harm from a nudge, providing the strongest direct evidence for the brief's distributional/manipulation-risk criterion (C5) in a non-employer, non-pension setting.
